newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST -- Powerful dlr/yen rally may fade in Q1.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST -- Powerful dlr/yen rally may fade in Q1.

text.p: The powerful rally that hurled the dollar above 121 yen for the first time in nearly four years could start to peter out this quarter, particularly if the U.S. trade gap with Japan begans to deteriorate, said analysts in a Reuter poll.
The greenback rocketed on Tuesday to 121.77 yen, a fresh 47-month high.

"Our bilateral trade flows with Japan, which improved markedly over the course of most of '95 and all of '96, have now improved about as much as they're going to," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
Liro said the U.S. bilateral trade gap with Japan will start widening again and conversely Japan's bilateral surplus will begin ballooning in the eyes of the Japanese.
"That shift in the trade flows from improving to deteriorating again will be a distinct negative (for the dollar)," Liro said.
A Reuter poll of 27 analysts, on average, predicted the dollar could fall to 117.69 yen by the end of the first quarter of 1997 and to 112.68 yen by the close of the fourth.
The decline is seen continuing in 1998, with the U.S. unit sliding to 110.53 yen by the end of the first quarter and 108.29 yen by the close of the fourth quarter.

In November, the latest month for which data are available, the U.S. trade gap with Japan shrank 12.9 percent to $4.32 billion. The cumulative deficit with Japan of $43.4 billion for the first 11 months of 1996 was the lowest for that period since 1991.

Robert Brusca, chief economist at Nikko Securities Co International Inc, said the dollar is currently benefiting from some "special factors", but he doubted the dollar will continue to rise as quickly as it has.

The "special factors" are weak economic conditions in Japan that had not been expected to persist as long as they have and a more-favorable-than-expected U.S. inflation environment, which probably will not last for the rest of the year, Brusca said.
"I think that we will wind up with a dollar whose run will end by the end of the first quarter or so," Brusca added.
